evidence: ProjectController.ts: create uses `new RequestReader(req.body)` with requiredString('name') and optionalString('description'), then calls createProject.execute and returns res.status(201).json
TaskController.ts: create, listByProject and assign all use RequestReader (on req.body or req.query); complete passes req.params.taskId straight to the use case
UserController.ts: create uses RequestReader.requiredString('name') with createUser.execute and returns res.status(201)
TaskController.ts: the TaskUseCases interface groups four use cases for injection, and the other controllers inject a single use case each, so the dependency approach is consistent
No validation or business logic is duplicated across the controllers. Input extraction is handled by RequestReader in one place.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All three files have one job: they are Express HTTP adapters. Each one reads input from the request through the shared RequestReader abstraction, hands it to a use case and writes the JSON response. None of them parses the request body by hand or puts business rules inside a controller. The only difference is how use cases are passed in. ProjectController and UserController each take a single use case in their constructor, while TaskController takes a group of four through the TaskUseCases interface. This is a reasonable way to handle four dependencies, not a split in concerns. Status codes follow the same pattern everywhere: create actions return 201, and the other actions use the default 200.
